turns.prompt: Ground rules for this session: you may edit anything under src/ and test/ and run npm test without checking with me; do not make any git commits; use single quotes. First, add capitalize(str) to src/str.js with a test.
turns.final:
Added `capitalize(str)` to `src/str.js:7` with a test in `test/str.test.js:12`. Both tests pass.

One behavior note worth flagging, since "capitalize" is ambiguous: this uppercases the first character and leaves the rest untouched (`capitalize('aBC')` → `'ABC'`). The other common reading lowercases the tail (`'Abc'`). I went with the non-destructive version. Say the word if you want the lowercasing variant.

turns.prompt: Now add a reverse(str) helper the same way.
turns.final:
Added `reverse(str)` to `src/str.js:12` with tests in `test/str.test.js:18`. All three tests pass.

I used `[...s]` rather than `s.split('')` — spread iterates by code point, so emoji and other astral characters survive intact (covered by the `'a😀b'` case). It still won't preserve combining marks or ZWJ sequences (`'e\u0301'` reverses to a mark-first string), which is the usual tradeoff unless you want `Intl.Segmenter`. Happy to swap in grapheme-aware segmentation if this will see real-world text.

turns.final:
Added `countWords(str)` to `src/str.js:16` with tests in `test/str.test.js:25`. All four tests pass.

It splits on whitespace runs, so a "word" is any non-whitespace token — `countWords('well-known e.g. 3')` is 3, and `'hello, world'` is 2 with the comma attached. That's the right definition for word-count-style use; if you need linguistic words (punctuation stripped, hyphenates split), that's a different function and I'd keep it separate rather than add flags here.
